Jewish Law. Known in Hebrew as halakhah, or the way to walk, it is the comprehensive system of religious, civil, and ethical obligations derived from the Torah and developed through centuries of Rabbinical interpretation. It governs every aspect of Jewish life, from dietary practices and Sabbath observance to marriage, commerce, and criminal justice. Far from being a static code, halakhah is a living tradition of interpretation and debate, with successive generations of rabbis adapting ancient principles to new circumstances while maintaining continuity with their sources.

Jewish law originates in the Written Torah, the Five Books of Moses, which contains six hundred thirteen commandments known as mitzvot, covering religious observance, ethical conduct, and ritual practice. The Oral Torah, later recorded in the Mishnah around 200 CE and expanded in the Talmud around 500 CE, represents Rabbinical interpretation, application, and extension of biblical law. Rabbinical authorities use specific hermeneutical methods to derive new applications from Torah, identifying contradictions, comparing similar cases, using verbal parallels, and reasoning from general principles to specific instances.

Major divisions of Jewish law include Kodashim or holy things, especially Temple sacrifice; Taharah or purity and impurity; Mo'ed or festivals and seasons; Nashim or women and family law; Nezikin or torts and criminal law; and Zeraim or agricultural laws. The Shulchan Aruch, or Set Table, compiled by Joseph Caro in the sixteenth century, became the standard code of Jewish law for Sephardic Jewry, while Ashkenazi communities developed their own custom-based variations.

Jewish law distinguishes between de-oraita or obligations from the Torah itself and de-rabbanan or Rabbinical ordinances intended to protect biblical law. The principle of pikuach nefesh, or saving a life, allows violation of almost any Jewish law if necessary to preserve human life, establishing human welfare as a supreme value. In modern times, different Jewish movements approach halakhah differently—Orthodox communities view it as binding and immutable, while Reform and Conservative movements see it as evolving.
